senses.def: pertaining to not being known
senses.comment: In Acts 17:23 the phrase ‘Unknown God’ may be simply rendered as ‘the god whom no one knows about,’ but in a number of languages the closest equivalent is ‘the god who has no name.’

senses.def: to be or to become disheartened and hence lack motivation

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: extension of time up to and beyond an expected point
(derivative of ἅλς ‘salt,’ 5.25) consisting of or pertaining to salt
senses.comment: It may be difficult in some languages to speak of ‘a salty spring’; rather, it may be necessary to say ‘a spring that produces water that tastes salty.’ In other instances one may have to say ‘a spring that flows from salty ground.’

senses.def: a room on the level above the ground floor (second story in American usage and first story in most other languages)
to send back to a previous location
to send on or up to some higher or appropriate authority
the blossom of a plant
senses.comment: In some languages it may be difficult to use generic expressions such as ‘flower’ or ‘plant.’ One may therefore be obliged to use a more specific designation of a type of flower which lasts for only a day or so. In James 1:10 it is the fragile and temporary nature of the blossom which is important in this figurative context.

senses.def: pertaining to being genuine and sincere, and hence lacking in pretense or show
pertaining to being healthy, with the implication of sound, proper functioning (in the NT with particular reference to the eyes)
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἁπλοῦς in Luke 11:34, see 57.107. See also 23.149.

senses.def: pertaining to willing and generous giving
senses.comment: In Matthew 6:22 and the corresponding passage in Luke 11:34, most scholars understand ἁπλοῦς in the sense of ‘to be healthy’ or ‘to be sound’ (see 23.132).

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning employing the base πνίγω[a] ‘to choke,’ 19.53) to cause the death of plants by other plants crowding them out and/or overshadowing them
to die as the result of drowning

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of moral excellence
senses.comment: It is possible, however, that ἀρετή in 2 Peter 1:3 denotes the manifestation of (divine) power (see 76.14).

senses.def: a manifestation of power characterized by excellence
pertaining to living without regard for religious belief or practice

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being arrogant as the result of self-will and stubbornness
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘arrogant’ may be expressed as ‘thinking one is so much better than everyone else’ or ‘always looking down on other people’ or ‘always saying, I am better.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: the continuous extent of time up to a point
senses.comment: The phrase εἰ μὴ ὅταν is often translated as ‘until’ (for example, μηδενὶ ἅ εἶδον διηγήσωνταιεἰ μὴ ὅταν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ ‘not to tell anybody what they have seen until the Son of Man has risen from death’ Mark 9:9), but this phrase may be analyzed as meaning ‘if it is not when,’ an expression which is semantically equivalent to ‘until.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time which is subsequent to a duration and simultaneous with another point of time
extension up to or as far as a goal

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time prior to another point of time

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time
a small, slender instrument, pointed on one end and with a hole at the other end, used in passing thread through cloth in sewing
senses.comment: There is no convincing evidence that the expression ‘eye of a needle’ in Matthew 19:24 and Luke 18:25 is a figurative name for a narrow gate. The reference to a camel passing through the eye of a needle is a case of rhetorical hyperbole, that is to say, a purposeful exaggeration to point out the extreme difficulty of the event referred to.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a councilor as a member of the Sanhedrin (see 11.80)

senses.comment: A number of languages distinguish clearly between various types of laughter: (1) laughter directed against some person as a form of ridicule; (2) laughter resulting from seeing some humorous event or as the result of listening to a humorous account; and (3) laughter which reflects happiness and joy. In Luke 6:21 and James 4:9 it is this third type of laughter which is relevant to the contexts.

senses.def: pertaining to wearing no clothing or being very scantily clothed
(a figurative extension of meaning of γυμνός[a] ‘naked,’ 49.22) easily able to be known in view of the fact that nothing is hidden
senses.comment: It is rare that one can employ in translating γυμνός b a term which literally means ‘naked,’ but it is possible to retain something of the metaphorical value by using a phrase such as ‘with nothing to cover’ or ‘with nothing which can be used to hide.’

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: (derivative of δέρμα ‘skin,’ 6.184) pertaining to being made of skin or leather
a verbal code, whether oral or written, as a basic means of communication
senses.comment: It is possible, though perhaps not probable, that διάλεκτος in Acts 2:6 may be understood not only as a language as such, but as a particular form of such a language, and hence would have a meaning of ‘manner of speaking’ or even ‘accent’ (see 33.102).

senses.def: to provide instruction in a formal or informal setting
senses.comment: The equivalent of ‘to teach’ in many languages is simply a causative form of a verb meaning ‘to learn’ or ‘to know,’ for example, ‘to cause to learn’ or ‘to cause to know.’ In choosing a term for ‘to teach’ it is important to avoid an expression which will denote merely classroom activity.

senses.def: (derivative of διδάσκω ‘to teach,’ 33.224) the content of what is taught
to try to learn the genuineness of something by examination and testing, often through actual use
glosses: to try to determine the genuineness of

senses.def: that which causes something to be known as true or genuine, in the sense of being what it appears to be
the proven or evident worth of someone or something
seventh in a series involving either time, space, or set
a set of favorable circumstances involving peace and tranquility
senses.comment: The meaning of ‘peace’ or ‘tranquility’ may be expressed in some languages in a negative form, for example, ‘to be without trouble’ or ‘to have no worries’ or ‘to sit down in one’s heart.’

senses.def: a state of freedom from anxiety and inner turmoil
senses.comment: ‘Peace’ in the sense of ‘freedom from worry’ is often expressed by means of an idiom, for example, ‘to sit down in the heart,’ ‘to rest in the liver,’ or ‘to be quiet in one’s inner self.’

senses.def: to cut in such a way as to cause separation
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκκόπτω[a] ‘to cut off,’ 19.18) to cause to cease by removing

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: behavior characterized by caprice and instability
senses.comment: In some instances ἐλαφρία may be rendered in 2 Corinthians 1:17 as ‘not thinking about what I was doing’ or ‘not keeping the same thoughts about what I was doing.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐμπλέκομαι ‘to become entangled,’ not occurring in the NT) to become so involved in some activity as to experience severe restrictions as to what one can do
a particular manner or way of thinking
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to render ‘way of thinking’ by a clause, for example, ‘how people think.’ In the case of 1 Peter 4:1, it may be necessary to translate ‘you too must strengthen yourselves by thinking just like Christ thought.’

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: that which is intended or purposed as the result of thinking
cardinal number, where there are sixty instances of a countable entity
senses.comment: Note that ἑξήκοντα in Matthew 13:8 is not ἑξηκόντακις ‘sixty times.’ The evident meaning here is that some of the seeds grew into plants which produced as many as a hundred seeds; others grew into plants which produced sixty seeds; and still others, only thirty seeds.

senses.subdomain: Units of Time with Reference to Other Units or Points of Time: Yesterday, Today, Next Day
senses.def: a day immediately following a previous day
to care for with diligent concern

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to give proper consideration to some issue or matter
glosses: to give attention so as to respond

senses.def: to cause to pour on or flow on

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: that which is good in the sense of beneficial
pertaining to events which measure up to their intended purpose
senses.comment: In the 65.23 contexts, βελτίων, καλῶς[b], εὖ[b], and εὖγε occur in highly elliptical constructions.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being a fitting or becoming manner of behavior
pertaining to being proper, with the implication of pleasing
(derivative of ζύμη ‘yeast,’ 5.11) to employ yeast in the process of making bread rise
the father of Abraham in the genealogy of Jesus
one of the judges of Israel
extension from a source which is away from the speaker

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time subsequent to another point of time
to lead or to bring down
to cause a boat to put in at a shore or to land
(technical, nautical terms) to go by ship toward the shore
to cause injury or harm by means of a statement regarded as having some supernatural power, often because a deity or supernatural force has been evoked
a position immediately or directly below a point of orientation, which is often left implicit
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not possible to speak of something ‘below’ without indicating precisely what is involved, but in the case of Acts 2:19 it would be irrelevant to say ‘marvels on the earth below the sky.’ Therefore, one may perhaps most satisfactorily translate this expression in Acts 2:19 as ‘marvels here on the earth.’

senses.def: extension toward a goal which is down or below
a type of spice derived from the bark of certain aromatic plants
senses.comment: In most languages κιννάμωμον is simply borrowed in a transliterated form. However, it is also possible to use a type of descriptive phrase, for example, ‘good-tasting bark’ or ‘flavoring bark.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the region of the body extending from the breast to the legs, especially when a person is in a seated position
senses.comment: The term κόλπος occurs in several idiomatic phrases in the NT. For example, the expression ‘who was in the bosom of the Father’ in John 1:18 denotes an association of intimacy and affection (see 34.18). In a context referring to the position of a person at a meal (as in John 13:23), κόλπος indicates an honored place (see 17.25). In Luke 16:22 κόλπος Ἀβραάμ signifies the heavenly abode (see 1.16).

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: the fold of a garment forming a type of pocket or container
a part of the sea which is partially enclosed by land
senses.comment: A ‘bay’ may be described as ‘a protected area of the sea’ or ‘a part of the sea protected by land.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: Abraham’s bosom) the heavenly abode, with the implication of close interpersonal relations
senses.comment: A literal rendering of κόλπος Ἀβραάμ as ‘the bosom of Abraham’ or ‘the lap of Abraham’ is often misleading. In some languages it may even suggest homosexuality, and in other cases it implies that Lazarus was either a baby or was changed into a baby in heaven. Since κόλπος Ἀβραάμ is generally interpreted as a reference to the eschatological heavenly feast, one may be justified in rendering Luke 16:22 as in TEV ‘the poor man died and was carried by the angels to sit beside Abraham at the feast in heaven.’ In some languages κόλπος Ἀβραάμ in this context is translated as ‘he was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side’ or ‘… to be with Abraham.’

senses.def: a court of justice for determining guilt or innocence
senses.comment: For languages which do not have technical terms for a court, it is usually possible to use some such phrase as ‘to be brought before a judge’ or ‘to have judges decide one’s case.’

senses.def: legal action taken in a court of law against someone
senses.comment: In most languages there are technical terms for lawsuits or cases in court, but where these do not exist, one may always use a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘to accuse someone before a judge’ or ‘to argue against someone in court’ or ‘to say in court that someone has done a person harm.’

senses.def: to take hold of something or someone, with or without force
senses.comment: A number of languages differ radically in terms for ‘taking hold of,’ depending upon whether force is employed, whether the object is a thing or an animate being, and whether the language incorporates into a verb of ‘taking hold of’ a classification as to the objects involved, for example, long and thin, round and flat, ball-like, angular, or lumpy.

senses.def: to acquire possession of something
senses.comment: In some languages ‘take’ in Matthew 5:40 may be best rendered as ‘go away with’ or ‘put it on as his own.’

senses.def: to receive or accept an object or benefit for which the initiative rests with the giver, but the focus of attention in the transfer is upon the receiver
to collect what is due (normally in terms of taxes and interest), with the possible implication of extortion (as in Luke 3:13)

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to make a choice of one or more possible alternatives
senses.comment: In a number of languages the choice of terms or expressions for ‘choosing’ or ‘selecting’ often depends upon either (1) what is chosen or selected or (2) the purpose for such a choice, for example, personal pleasure, rational evaluation, or outright prejudice.|It is also possible to interpret λαμβάνω in Hebrews 5:1 as meaning ‘to acquire, to obtain’ (see λαμβάνω[b], 57.55).

senses.def: to come to believe something and to act in accordance with such a belief

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of λαμβάνω[a] ‘to take hold,’ 18.1) to take advantage of someone by trickery or deception
glosses: to take advantage of by trickery

senses.def: to experience some event or state, often with the implication of something negatively valued
to cause to experience, normally implying something grievous
senses.comment: It is, of course, possible to understand λαμβάνω in Mark 14:65 in a more or less literal sense (see 18.1) and thus to translate this expression as ‘the guards took him and slapped him.’

senses.def: to put on an article of clothing
a marker of an agent relation with numerable events, with the implication of having assumed some initiative
(an idiom, literally: to take a rule, to receive a rule) to receive from someone else the power or authority to reign as a king
(an idiom, literally: to take courage) to become confident or courageous in the face of real or possible danger

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to take face) to make unjust distinctions between people by treating one person better than another
senses.comment: ‘To show favoritism’ or ‘to be partial’ is expressed in an idiomatic manner in some languages, for example, ‘to look only upon a person’s face,’ ‘to call a sparrow a chicken,’ or ‘to give one’s clansman the best piece of meat.’

senses.def: (a productive idiomatic expression, literally: to take one’s cross) to be prepared to endure severe suffering, even to the point of death
glosses: to be prepared to suffer even unto death
senses.comment: The idiom ‘to carry one’s cross’ or ‘to take up one’s cross’ involves a number of important features of meaning. Unfortunately, this expression is frequently not understood correctly by many people who hear it or even use it. One reason for this is the actual absence of crucifixion in modern society. If a literal translation is to be employed, then some marginal note will probably be necessary in order to indicate clearly the full implications of such a statement.

senses.def: to attempt to do something, with the implication of not succeeding
senses.comment: In a number of languages expressions such as πειράζω[d], πειράομαι, and πεῖραν λαμβάνω may be expressed as to start to do something, but not be able to or to think that one can do something, but discover it is impossible.

senses.def: pertaining to being splendid, with the implication of luxurious
senses.comment: In Revelation 18:14 λαμπρός (79.20) and λιπαρός serve primarily to reinforce one another.

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a large quantity, involving extent
the upper range of a scale of extent, with the possible implication of importance in relevant contexts
a large size, relative to the norm for the class of objects in question

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: pertaining to being great in terms of status
pertaining to being surprising in view of being important
a degree which surpasses in some manner a point on an explicit or implicit scale of extent

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: pertaining to having a higher status in comparison to something else

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to the older of two objects
senses.comment: In some languages ‘the older will serve the younger’ must be rendered as ‘the one who was born first will serve the one who was born later.’

senses.def: pertaining to being extremely important

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively long duration of time
persons of important or high status
to change one’s way of life as the result of a complete change of thought and attitude with regard to sin and righteousness
senses.comment: Though in English a focal component of repent is the sorrow or contrition that a person experiences because of sin, the emphasis in μετανοέω and μετάνοια seems to be more specificaly the total change, both in thought and behavior, with respect to how one should both think and act. Whether the focus is upon attitude or behavior varies somewhat in different contexts. Compare, for example, Luke 3:8, Hebrews 6:1, and Acts 26:20.

senses.def: a Greek monetary unit worth one hundred denarii
a disciple of Jesus
common and official currency
the group of servants working in a particular household
to express openly one’s allegiance to a proposition or person
senses.comment: It is often extremely difficult, if not impossible, to translate ὁμολογέω[a], ὁμολογία, and ἐξομολογέω[b] by the usual expression for ‘confess,’ since this would usually imply that one has done something wrong. It is normally necessary, therefore, to employ quite a different type of relationship, usually involving a public utterance and an expression of confidence or allegiance. For example, in Matthew 10:32 it may be necessary to translate ‘whoever tells people publicly that he is loyal to me, I will tell my Father that I am loyal to that person.’ Similarly, in Hebrews 10:23 one may translate ‘let us hold on to the hope in which we have told people we have such confidence.’ Likewise, in Romans 15:9 one may translate ‘therefore I will tell the Gentiles how I have put my confidence in you.’

senses.def: to acknowledge a fact publicly, often in reference to previous bad behavior
senses.comment: In Philippians 2:11 the statement πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσηται ὅτι κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός (‘that everyone may confess that Jesus Christ is Lord’) means simply to acknowledge a fact publicly, and in this instance there is no implication of previous bad behavior.

senses.def: to make an emphatic declaration, often public, and at times in response to pressure or an accusation
a relatively high elevation of land, in contrast with βουνός hill (1.48), which is by comparison somewhat lower
senses.comment: Terms referring to mountains, hills, or mounds inevitably reflect the nature of the surrounding landscape. For example, in the flat marshlands of the Central Sudan, an elevation called Doleib Hill is only some three or four feet above the surrounding area, but in the Himalayas elevations of land some ten or twelve thousand feet are still regarded as hills in contrast with the mountains. In the choice of receptor language terms for ὄρος and βουνός (1.48), one must seek expressions which suggest corresponding differences. What is important is relative size, not an exact correspondence to biblical geography. It may, however, be necessary in some instances to introduce a footnote to describe the approximate height of certain biblical mountains or hills.

senses.def: the payment made to soldiers as ration money
money which is needed for living expenses
senses.comment: ὀψώνιον in 2 Corinthians 11:8 may be rendered as ‘money on which to live’ or ‘money for food and lodging.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὀψώνιον[a] ‘a soldier’s wages,’ 57.166) the end result from some activity, viewed as something which one receives in return
to ask for with urgency, even to the point of demanding

senses.subdomain: Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention
senses.def: to not pay attention to
glosses: to refuse to pay attention to

senses.subdomain: Belong To, Be Included in the Membership of, Be Excluded From
senses.def: to refuse to accept one into a particular association
senses.comment: A strictly literal translation of παραιτέομαι in this context might be misunderstood, since it could suggest that younger widows were to be rejected from membership in the church. It may therefore be necessary to specify the particular relationships by translating ‘but do not accept younger widows in the list of those to receive support from the church.’

senses.def: purposely to avoid association with someone
glosses: to have nothing to do with

senses.def: to refuse to listen to and hence to disobey
senses.comment: It would be a mistake to translate παρακούω[a], παρακοή, and παραιτέομαι[e] as meaning nothing more than ‘not to listen to.’ The meaning is clearly ‘to refuse to listen to’ or ‘to refuse to pay attention to,’ and hence ‘to disobey.’ It may therefore be best in a number of instances to translate ‘to refuse to obey.’

senses.def: a means of providing comfort or consolation
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand παρηγορία in Colossians 4:11 as meaning ‘help’ (see 35.14).

senses.def: that which constitutes a means of help
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand παρηγορία in Colossians 4:11 as meaning ‘comfort’ (see 25.155).

senses.def: the mother of one’s spouse
senses.comment: In a number of languages the semantic components of ‘mother-in-law’ must be made explicit. For example, in Mark 1:30 one may translate ‘the mother-in-law of Simon’ as ‘the mother of Simon’s wife.’

senses.def: a degree which is considerably in excess of some point on an implied or explicit scale of extent
to increase considerably the extent of an activity or state, with the implication of the result being an abundance
senses.comment: It may be difficult in some languages to speak of ‘sin increasing,’ but in Romans 5:20 one can say ‘where people sinned more and more.’|In 2 Corinthians 4:15 the increase would be in the instances of God’s grace extending to more and more people.

senses.def: to cause an increase in the degree of some experience or state
senses.comment: It would seem that πλεονάσαι and περισσεύσαι in 1 Thessalonians 3:12 simply reinforce the meaning of intense degree. It is assumed that these two expressions are not completely synonymous, but it is difficult to determine precisely how they may contrast. It may simply be that περισσεύσαι is somewhat more emphatic.

senses.def: to exist or be in abundance
senses.comment: The two participial forms, ὑπάρχοντα (see 57.2) and πλεονάζοντα, are coalesced in the translation as ‘have … in abundance.’|In a number of languages the equivalent of this expression in 2 Peter 1:8 might be ‘if you have a great many of these’ or ‘for if these are big with you.’

senses.def: to have more than enough to meet one’s needs
pertaining to being of great value or worth, implying in some contexts a monetary scale

senses.subdomain: In Front Of, Face To Face, In Back Of, Behind
senses.def: a position in front of an object, whether animate or inanimate, which is regarded as having a spacial orientation of front and back

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time prior to another point of time
marker of primary importance

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: before the doors) a point of time subsequent to another point of time and indicating imminence, that is to say, the subsequent event is regarded as almost begun

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: an exceedingly long period of time from an assumed beginning up to the present

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: before the face, equivalent in meaning to πρό[b] ‘before,’ 67.17, but a somewhat more elaborate phrase rhetorically) a point of time, possibly only a short time before another point of time
to bring or lead into the presence of someone
glosses: to bring into the presence of

senses.def: to move toward a reference point, with a possible implication in certain contexts of a reciprocal relationship between the person approaching and the one who is approached
that which is offered to God in religious activity
the light, flames, and heat produced by the burning of materials
senses.comment: Though the ancient view of the elements would lead to classification of this occurrence of πῦρ (2 Peter 3:7) as referring to a natural substance, the fact that the reference is to a particular event means that in many languages one must speak of a ‘burning,’ and this must be expressed frequently by a verb or participle rather than by a noun, for example, ‘for destruction by being burned up.’

senses.def: a pile or heap of burning material
senses.comment: The Greek phrase ἅψαντες … πυράν ‘to kindle a fire’ is best rendered in a number of languages by a single verb meaning ‘to make a fire,’ and in some languages it is strange to speak of a ‘fire’ without indicating the type of material which is being burned. Hence, in Acts 28:2 the appropriate equivalent would be ‘they caused some sticks to burn.’|In some languages a very important distinction is made between two functionally different kinds of fire, one used for getting rid of refuse and the other used for warming oneself. Fire as a destructive agent, mentioned frequently in the book of Revelation (Revelation 8:5 and Revelation 20:10), may require quite a different term from what is used in speaking of a fire for the purpose of warming a person or heating an object.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to throw fire) to cause discord and contention
senses.comment: Some translators have preferred to retain the literal rendering of this expression in Luke 12:49, since this seems to be necessary in view of the larger figurative context, which speaks of ‘how I wish it were already kindled’ (τί θέλω εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη). A strictly literal translation may, however, be understood in a completely physical sense, namely, ‘to set the world on fire.’ There are a number of quite diverse interpretations of the significance of this expression in Luke 12:49. Some have assumed, for example, that it refers to the fire of Pentecost.

senses.def: (derivative of σεβάζομαι ‘to worship,’ 53.53) a place of worship
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σέβασμα in Acts 17:23, see 53.55.

senses.def: (derivative of σεβάζομαι ‘to worship,’ 53.53) an object which is worshiped
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σέβασμα in Acts 17:23, see 53.54.

senses.def: a portable dwelling of cloth and/or skins, held up by poles and fastened by cords to stakes
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘tent’ is simply ‘a house made of cloth.’ One should avoid terms which would imply a military tent or a temporary shelter used only on vacations or holidays. In OT times such tents were permanent dwellings of nomadic groups and were moved from place to place as livestock were transferred from one pasture area to another.

senses.def: the relatively large tent used as a central place of worship by the Jews prior to the building of the Temple
senses.comment: In a number of languages σκηνή[b] may be rendered as ‘the largest tent in which God lived’ or ‘the large tent for worshiping God’ or ‘the holy tent.’ In selecting a proper designation for σκηνή[b], it is important to indicate that the function of σκηνή[b] was essentially the same as that of the Temple; it was only a different type of construction and not a difference of use or of religious relevance.|Since σκηνή[b] refers to one unique object, it is essentially equivalent to a title.

senses.def: a porous material used to absorb liquid
senses.comment: In the only type of NT context in which σπόγγος occurs (Matthew 27:48; Mark 15:36; John 19:29), it serves as a container for cheap wine offered to Jesus on the cross.

senses.def: to cause something to turn
to cause something to turn into or to become something else
to carry something back to a point where it had been formerly
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret στρέφω in Matthew 27:3 as ‘pay back’ or ‘giving back money’ (see 57.157).

senses.def: to return a payment
senses.comment: It is possible to interpret στρέφω in Matthew 27:3 as simply meaning ‘to bring back’ or ‘to take back’ (see 15.195).

senses.def: to reject an existing relation of association
to turn around to or toward
to change one’s belief, with focus upon that to which one turns
senses.comment: In analyzing the meaning of στρέφω[g], ἐπιστρέφω[b], and ἐπιστροφή[a] in such passages as Matthew 18:3, John 12:40, and Acts 7:39, it is difficult to determine the extent to which belief or behavior is primarily in focus. In the case of 1 Peter 2:25, one could certainly argue that the emphasis is upon the interpersonal relationship. It is therefore essential in rendering these terms not to narrow the meaning too much, for in this way one would certainly do violence to certain crucial semantic features.|For another interpretation of στρέφομαι in Matthew 18:3, see 41.50.

any kind of food or nourishment
senses.comment: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as Matthew 6:11 as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering Luke 4:4 (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of Luke 4:4 is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

senses.def: a structure for enclosing an open area
senses.comment: In practically all societies there is some type of fence, wall, or barrier employed to surround fields. In some instances this may consist of piled up logs or sticks; in other instances the wall may be made of packed dirt or of laid-up stone. What is important, however, is not the form, but the function, and therefore one may often use a descriptive expression, for example, ‘a barrier to surround a field,’ sometimes described as ‘a barrier to keep animals out of the field.’|φραγμός[a] is also used figuratively of the Law, which constituted a barrier between Jews and Gentiles: τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ ‘a wall of separation’ or ‘barrier’ Ephesians 2:14. In Ephesians 2:14 φραγμός[a] may be rendered as ‘a wall to keep apart’ or ‘a wall to divide’ (see 34.39).
